L19:     27.1 KEEPING FEET WARM IN WET COLD AREAS (added), a. Importance of keeping feet warm and dry. Keeping the feet warm is a vital problem in all wet cold areas, such as Europe in the winter months. Cold wet feet may lead to trench foot and make a soldier a casualty, unfit for duty. It is easier to keep the feet warm in dry snow at zero than in mud and slush at 35°. It is much easier to keep warm in cold, dry weather than it is under -fairly cold, wet conditions.
L20: Footgear that will give adequate protection at 25°, if it is dry, will fail at 40° if it is wet.
L21:     b.	Types of shoes for wet cold areas. To keep the feet warm in wet cold weather, a soldier must have the right type of footgear, fitted properly and worn with the correct sock combination. In cold wet weather he should wear either a pair of overshoes in addition to his service shoes or his combat boots (par. 33.1), or a pair of shoepacs (par. 33).
L22:     c.	Why wet feet are cold feet. Wet feet are cold feet. Footgear does not generate heat. It merely is an insulator which holds in the heat of the foot. In well-fitted shoes, insulation depends on thickness. Dry, clean socks have a certain degree of thickness which is reduced when they become matted. Moisture or dirt allows the wool in socks to get matted so that they become thinner and, therefore, give less protection. Dry socks and dry boots are good msulators. Water is a poor insulator.
L23: Therefore, when footgear is wet, a great real of heat is lost and the feet become cold. Just as the water inside a canteen is cooled by the evaporation of the moisture from a wet canteen cover, so the feet are chilled by the evaporation of moisture from footgear.
L24:     d.	How the feet become wet from the inside. Moisture comes either from the inside (the foot) or from the outside. There are two kinds of perspiration that comes from the foot, the kind that drops off when one is overheated and a smaller continuous flow. When overheated, one sweats visibly. In cold weather this does not necessarily come from wearing too many socks.
L25: Three or four pairs of socks can be worn with no perceptible sweating if the rest of the body is kept cool by the removal of the muffler or sweater, or by the opening of the field jacket when one is moving fast or working hard. If the body is kept from overheating, the feet will not sweat excessively but they will perspire a little. Perspiration occurs on the

L30:     soles of the feet and under the armpits even when one is cold. This kind of perspiration collects, especially when water-tight shoes such as shoepacs or overshoes are worn. These do not “make the feet sweat”, but they do keep in all the moisture that is produced and this accumulates hour by hour. That is the reason the socks will have to be dried even if the boots are waterproof.
L31:     e.	Keeping dry from the outside. Some men receive considerable protection from outside moisture in service shoes or combat boots; others, very little. The difference lies in the care that is given the shoes. Dubbin will help to waterproof leather shoes and will keep them softer, more comfortable and less likely to wear out. The boots should be cleaned, dried (but not completely), and dubbin applied, spread, and rubbed in well.
L32: Whenever possible avoid walking through or standing in water, wet snow or mud. Water in trenches or foxholes can frequently be bailed out. Pieces of wood, branches or rocks can be used to stand on.
L33:     f.	What to do about wet cold feet. If the feet should become wet and cold, scrunch up the toes, move the ankles around, stamp the feet and exercise as much as possible. At every opportunity remove shoes and socks and dry the feet thoroughly. Never rub or massage the feet when they are uncomfortably cold or when they are at all numb. Pain and numbness may mean the beginning of trench foot, and a medical officer should be seen at once.
L34: Remove shoes and socks at least once a day and replace the wet socks with dry ones. If no dry ones are available, wring out the ones that are being worn and put them back on. Dust foot powder on the feet twice a day. Sleep or rest with the feet at a higher level than the head, when possible. Always keep a change of dry socks. Take advantage of every opportunity to dry shoes, socks, and, if shoepacs are worn, insoles (pars. 28 and 29).
L35:     33.1 BOOTS, SERVICE, COMBAT, AND SHOES, SERVICE (added), a. Socks and sock combinations for cold-climate wear. The following socks and sock combinations are suggested for wear with shoes, service, and boots, service, combat, under cold-climate conditions:
L36:     (1)	2 pairs of socks, wool, cushion sole
L37:     (2)	1 pair of socks, wool, cushion sole and

L40:     (4)	1 pair of socks, wool, heavy
L41:     Combination (1) is the preferred sock combination, but any of the above sock combinations (which are listed in the order of desirability) is satisfactory. However, they must be worn with properly fitting shoes. If more than one sock is worn, the shoe must necessarily be larger. Be sure

L50:     the shoes are not tight. A properly fitting sock will be filled by the foot without apparent tightness or excessive fullness. There should be an excess length clearance at the toe of a new sock of about % inch to allow for shrinkage. A sock that is too tight or too short may restrict the circulation and thus cause the feet to become cold. If two pairs of socks are worn, the outside pair should be at least one-half size longer than the inside pair.
L51: Socks in addition to those listed in these four combinations should not be worn with shoes, service, or boots, service, combat, since the wearing of too many socks may restrict the circulation and cause the feet to become colder than if one of the above sock combinations is worn. Should the feet swell because of extreme cold, it may be advisable to remove one pair of socks or to loosen the shoe laces.
L52:     b.	Fit of boots and shoes to be worn in co‘d dimates. The fit of boots, service, combat, and shoes, service, for wear in a cold climate must never be so tight or so short as to restrict the circulation and reduce the flow of warm blood to the feet. Shoes, service, and boots, service, combat are ordinarily fitted to be worn over one pair of socks, wool, light, or socks wool, cushion sole.
L53: If additional socks are worn with leather boots or shoes in cold weather in accordance with sock combinations (1), (2), (3), or (4) above, a careful shoe- and sock-fitting check should be made to make sure that the shoes and socks are not too tight or too short. This will also apply to the fit of all other boots, shoes, and sock combinations which are worn in a cold climate.
L54: The boot, shoe, and sock combinations which will be worn by enlisted personnel in cold climates should be checked for proper fit in accordance with the above, and with AR 850-125, 9 June 1943. Whenever troops are being equipped at bases for field duty under cold-climate conditions, this fitting check should be made. Prior to departure for duty in the field, such enlisted personnel should be instructed in the proper care of their feet, and the proper use of available socks and footwear.
L55:     c.	Drying shoes. Use every opportunity to dry shoes. Sun and wind will dry them even at fairly cold temperatures. When not on the move, they can be placed in sunny spots where circulating air will strike them. The use of fires, one-burner gasoline stove, or fuel tablets is sometimes permissible. Great care should be taken to avoid burning the shoes or ruining them by too great heat. Always hold the shoes in the bare hands so that the heat will be felt before it burns or shrinks the leather.
L56: If it is too hot for the hands, it is too hot for the leather. When drying them, never put the hands inside the shoes, nor prop them on a stick nor set them near the fire. Never try to warm the feet with shoes on. The shoes will burn before the feet feel warmer.

L107:     4.1. KEEPING ACTIVE (Added), a. One of the basic principles for keeping warm is to keep active. The main objective of keeping active is to maintain good blood circulation throughout the body. Clenching and wiggling of fingers and toes, swift movement of the arms and legs, and ordinary walking or stepping up and down are extremely helpful.
L108:     b.	To keep active does not mean overexertion or exercising the muscles to the point of getting hot and sweaty. Sweating and exhaustion must be avoided.

L178:     40.1. MliTENS, ARCTIC (Added), a. Purpose. The arctic mitten (fig. 13.1) is designed to be worn over the trigger finger insert mitten in extremely cold conditions. It consists of two parts, a leather-palmed cotton shell mitten and a duffel insert. Ordinarily both are worn together (put on together and taken off together). but must be separated for drying purposes. However, if it is too warm, remove either the duffel insert or the trigger finger insert mitten before sweating starts.
L179:     Figure 13.1. Mittens, arctic.
L180:     b. Wear. I here is no trigger finger in the arctic mitten, because the three layers (two of arctic mittens and one of insert mitten) could not be slipped into a trigger guard. Therefore, the arctic mitten is removed before firing. This exposes the trigger finger insert mitten. I he arctic mitten hangs from the cord which runs up the sleeves and around the neck. I he pile on the back of the arctic mitten adds to the warmth of the mitten and is useful for warming the face.
L181: To warm the face, place the back of the mitten against the chilled part.
L182:     c. Care. To dry, separate the leather-palmed cotton shell mitten and the duffel insert. Dry these in same manner that any mittens are dried.
L183:     52.1. MASK, FACE, COLD WEATHER (Added), a. Purpose. This face mask is worn in subzero weather when facing the wind, such as when on guard or when driving an open vehicle. It is not usually desirable to wear the mask when engaging in violent activity. Proper use of the parka hood often eliminates the need for the mask. If glasses are worn, they may be worn under goggles over the mask.
